meaning: “Luckily…, or else it would have been bad.” Relief mixed with a scolding or warning tone.
connection: Plain form + からいいようなものの (nouns / na-adjectives: 〜だからいいようなものの)

senses.label: Luckily…, but otherwise
senses.meaning: The first part is a lucky outcome; the second part points out that it could have been much worse, or criticizes someone. Like “It's a good thing…, otherwise…”. The speaker is relieved but not satisfied, and often sounds reproachful.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form + からいいようなものの; noun / na-adjective + だからいいようなものの. The second part often uses 「〜ところだった」, 「〜たらどうするんだ」 or 「気をつけなさい」.
examples: It's lucky the injury was minor. One wrong move and it would have been a major accident.
Good thing we had insurance. Otherwise we'd have paid for the whole repair ourselves.
It's fine because today's a holiday, but on a weekday you'd be totally late.

senses.label: Past form
senses.meaning: When the event is already over, it is often said as 「〜からよかったものの」. Same meaning: “It was lucky that…, so nothing happened.” In speech this is more common than 「いいようなものの」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + からよかったものの
examples: Luckily nobody noticed, but you mustn't say something that rude.
The rain stopped right away, luckily, but climbing a mountain without even an umbrella is reckless.

notes: The second part must be criticism, a warning, or an imagined bad outcome; the pattern cannot express plain happiness: ✕「合格したからいいようなものの、本当にうれしい」→ ○「合格したからいいようなものの、もっと早く準備すべきだった」.
The first part must be a lucky good outcome; if it is something bad, the pattern is impossible: ✕「失敗したからいいようなものの、…」→ ○「失敗したものの、…」.

It carries a scolding tone. Saying 「〜からいいようなものの…」 to a boss or client amounts to blaming them to their face and is very rude; to a superior, say something like 「大事に至らず何よりでした」 first and then offer your suggestion gently.
Nouns and na-adjectives need 「だ」: ✕「休日からいいようなものの」→ ○「休日だからいいようなものの」.

daily.title: Parents scolding a child
daily.description: The child got into trouble but nothing serious happened. The parents are relieved but still scold.
daily.example: Good thing you weren't hurt, but running into the road is dangerous, isn't it?

daily.title: A friend's lost wallet comes back
daily.description: A careless friend lost something and someone returned it. The speaker tells them to be careful.
daily.example: Lucky someone turned it in to the police box, but you need to be more careful.

work.title: A boss points out a mistake
work.description: A subordinate almost sent the wrong email but caught it in time. The boss gives a serious warning.
work.example: It's good you noticed before sending, but don't neglect your checks.

work.title: Incident review
work.description: An internal meeting looks back at a near miss that almost caused losses.
work.example: Luckily there was no damage this time, but we need to review our management system.

etymology: Made of reason 「から」 + 「いい」 (good) + 「ようなもの」 (something like) + the contrastive 「ものの」 (although). Literally “because of…, it's sort of good, but…”, which became the set phrase “luckily…, otherwise…”.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: Same origin: both end in the concessive 「ものの」. 「〜ものの」 is a general “although…”, and the first part can be good or bad (「買ったものの、使っていない」); 「からいいようなものの」 requires the first part to be a lucky good outcome and the second to be criticism or “it nearly went wrong”.

similar.title: 〜てよかった
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express relief at “luckily…”. 「〜てよかった」 simply expresses gladness or relief and can end there; 「からいいようなものの」 always adds a reproach or warning after the relief and cannot express joy on its own.

similar.title: 〜ものを
similar.explanation: Both carry dissatisfaction or blame. 「〜ものを」 targets what was not done, meaning “it would have been fine if only…, but…” (「言ってくれればよかったものを」); 「からいいようなものの」 targets what luckily did not go wrong and warns the other person to be careful next time.

formation: Taken apart, it is 「〜から」 (because) + 「いい」 (fine, no harm done) + 「ような」 (like, sort of) + the concessive 「ものの」 (although). 「〜からいい」 first gives the judgment “it is fine thanks to this one thing”; 「ような」 makes that “fine” vague, only “it seems fine, more or less”, without really affirming it; and the final 「ものの」 turns the sentence around. So the weight of the whole sentence is in the second half: the relief is only a lead-in, and what the speaker really wants to say is “actually it was dangerous” or “you shouldn't have done that”. That is why the second part must be criticism, a warning or an imagined bad outcome. For something already over, change 「いい」 to the past form and you get 「〜からよかったものの」, with the structure unchanged.

meaning: A set phrase made of two adjectives with opposite meanings: “whether A or B, the result is the same.”
connection: Adjective stem + かれ + opposite adjective stem + かれ (遅かれ早かれ／多かれ少なかれ／善かれ悪しかれ)

senses.label: Sooner or later
senses.meaning: 「遅かれ早かれ」 means “sooner or later”. The timing is unclear, but it will definitely happen. Often used to predict a negative or inevitable result.
senses.connection: 遅かれ早かれ + guess / inevitability (〜だろう, 〜ものだ, 〜ことになる)
examples: Lies always come out sooner or later.
At this rate, the company will hit a dead end sooner or later.

senses.label: More or less
senses.meaning: 「多かれ少なかれ」 means “more or less, to some degree”. The degree differs, but everyone has it.
senses.connection: 多かれ少なかれ + 〜ている／〜ものだ (often with 「誰でも」, 「みんな」)
examples: Everyone has worries to some degree.
People grow up influenced by their parents, more or less.

senses.label: For better or worse
senses.meaning: 「善かれ悪しかれ」 means “for better or worse”. It states a fact without judging it. Also written 「良かれ悪しかれ」.
senses.connection: 善かれ悪しかれ／良かれ悪しかれ + objective fact
examples: For better or worse, the internet has greatly changed our lives.
For better or worse, he is the most famous person in this town.

notes: Only a few fixed set phrases exist, such as 「遅かれ早かれ」, 「多かれ少なかれ」 and 「善かれ悪しかれ」. You cannot coin new ones: ✕「高かれ安かれ」→ ○「高くても安くても」.
「良かれと思って」 means “thinking it would be good for the person”, and is usually followed by “but it backfired”. It does not mean “good or bad”, so do not confuse the two.
「遅かれ早かれ」 is followed by something that is sure to happen, usually something bad. Telling someone 「遅かれ早かれ失敗しますよ」 sounds like a curse and is very rude.

daily.title: Urging a friend to come clean
daily.description: A friend is hiding something from their family. The speaker urges them to say it soon.
daily.example: They'll find out sooner or later, so you'd better tell them early.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is stressed out. The speaker says everyone feels the same.
daily.example: Work stress? Everyone has it to some degree.

work.title: Business analysis report
work.description: A report points out that a change is unavoidable.
work.example: The effects of population decline will reach every industry sooner or later.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator objectively assesses the impact of a policy.
work.example: For better or worse, this reform became a turning point for Japanese society.

etymology: 「〜かれ」 is the imperative of classical adjectives (a contraction of 「〜くあれ」), meaning “let it be…”. Two opposite imperatives side by side mean “be it A, be it B”, which led to “either way”.

similar.title: 〜であれ／〜であれ〜であれ
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「あれ」 in 「であれ」 and the 「かれ」 (= 「くあれ」) are both the imperative of the old verb 「あり」, and both mean “whether it is… or not”. 「であれ」 attaches to nouns and can be swapped freely (「男であれ女であれ」); 「〜かれ〜かれ」 is limited to a few fixed adjective pairs.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うが〜まいが／〜(よ)うと〜まいと
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “whatever happens…”. 「(よ)うが〜まいが」 contrasts the affirmative and negative of the same verb (「行こうが行くまいが」) and can be used freely; 「〜かれ〜かれ」 uses a pair of opposite adjectives and is a frozen idiom.

similar.title: 〜にしろ〜にしろ・〜にしても〜にしても
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “whether A or B, …”. 「〜にしろ〜にしろ」 attaches to many kinds of nouns and verbs and is flexible (「賛成にしろ反対にしろ」); 「〜かれ〜かれ」 is used only in fixed combinations and is more literary.

formation: 「〜かれ」 is the imperative of a classical adjective, contracted from 「〜く」 + 「あれ」 (the imperative of 「あり」): 「遅くあれ」 → 「遅かれ」. The imperative here is not a real command but a permissive tone, “even if it is… that is fine”. Lining up the permissive forms of a pair of opposite words, “late or early”, covers every possibility, and so you get “whichever it is, the result is the same”. Because it is a fossil left over from classical conjugation, only a few high-frequency pairs of opposites survive in modern Japanese, and you cannot freely coin new ones.

meaning: The classical auxiliary 「ごとし」: “like…, as if…”. It can also give examples or show contempt.
connection: Noun + の + ごとし／ごとく／ごとき; verb plain form (+ が) + ごとし／ごとく; noun + ごとき (contempt)

senses.label: Simile: like…
senses.meaning: A literary version of 「〜ようだ」. 「ごとし」 ends a sentence, 「ごとく」 modifies verbs, and 「ごとき」 modifies nouns. Common in proverbs, literature and written texts.
senses.connection: Noun + の / verb dictionary or ta-form (+ が) + ごとし／ごとく／ごとき
examples: Time flies like an arrow.
He drank sake as if it were water.
Those dreamlike days passed in the blink of an eye.

senses.label: As stated…
senses.meaning: 「〜のごとく」 after nouns like 「前述」, 「周知」 or 「例年」 means “as…”. Equivalent to 「〜のように」, used in formal writing.
senses.connection: 前述の／上記の／周知の／例年の／次の + ごとく
examples: As mentioned above, this method also has drawbacks.
As is well known, Japan is a country with many earthquakes.

senses.label: Contempt / humility
senses.meaning: 「Noun + ごとき」 attached to a person or thing means “the likes of…, a mere…”. About others it sounds contemptuous; about yourself it sounds humble.
senses.connection: Noun (person / thing) + ごとき (+ に／が／の)
examples: Could someone like me really handle such an important role?
As if I'd lose to the likes of you!
I can't take a day off work for a mere cold.

notes: When 「ごとき」 follows a person directly, it is contemptuous: 「お前ごとき」 means “a nobody like you” and is extremely rude toward others. Only when used about yourself (「私ごとき」) is it humble. Getting the direction wrong has serious consequences.
A comparison takes 「の」; contempt does not: 「夢のごとき日々」 means “days like a dream”, while 「私ごとき」 means “a humble person like me”. With or without 「の」, the meaning changes.
The form must match what follows: 「ごとし」 at the end of a sentence, 「ごとく」 before a verb, 「ごとき」 before a noun: ✕「夢のごとく日々」→ ○「夢のごとき日々」.
It expresses only comparison or example, never conjecture as 「ようだ」 can: ✕「雨が降るごとし」 (meant as “it looks like rain”) → ○「雨が降るようだ」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel uses a simile to describe a scene or a character.
daily.example: Her snow-white skin glowed in the moonlight.

daily.title: Quoting a proverb
daily.description: Quoting a proverb when amazed at how fast time passes.
daily.example: End of the year already? Time really does fly like an arrow.

daily.title: Humbly declining
daily.description: Given a big responsibility, the speaker uses humble wording to show reluctance.
daily.example: Someone like me as leader? I couldn't possibly.

work.title: Linking ideas in formal documents
work.description: Referring back to earlier content in a report or paper.
work.example: As stated above, this year's sales exceeded last year's.

work.title: Formal speeches
work.description: Quoting a famous saying in a formal address for impact.
work.example: As the saying goes, “Too much is as bad as too little.”

etymology: 「ごとし」 is a classical auxiliary of comparison, written 「如し」. It is generally thought to come from 「こと」 meaning “same”. Modern 「〜ようだ」 took over its function, while 「ごとし」 survives in writing and proverbs.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「ごとし」 is the classical-language counterpart of 「ようだ」 (「ごとし／ごとく／ごとき」 ≈ 「ようだ／ように／ような」). But 「ようだ」 can also express conjecture, whereas 「ごとし」 expresses only comparison or example and is used only in writing and proverbs.

similar.title: 〜かのようだ
similar.explanation: Both can mean “as if… (though it is not so)”. 「かのようだ」 is modern written language (「まるで夢であるかのようだ」); 「〜がごとく」 is more archaic and appears mostly in literature and speeches.

similar.title: 〜ように (as stated)
similar.explanation: Same meaning: 「前述のように」 = 「前述のごとく」. 「のごとく」 is more formal and written, and is common in papers and official documents.

formation: 「ごとし」 is a classical auxiliary, generally thought to come from 「こと（同）」, meaning “the same”, plus the adjective ending 「し」, so its original sense is “the same as…”. That is why it naturally expresses comparison and example: 「光陰矢のごとし」 = “time flies like an arrow”. It conjugates like an adjective: 「ごとし」 ends a sentence, the continuative 「ごとく」 modifies verbs, and the attributive 「ごとき」 modifies nouns, matching modern 「ようだ／ように／ような」. The contemptuous use classes the object as “something of that sort”, implying “nothing more than that kind”, hence the belittling; used about yourself it becomes humble.

meaning: “Only A, never B”: strongly denies the opposite of the first part. 「〜こそあれ」 can also mean “there may be A, but…”.
connection: Noun / verb masu-stem + こそすれ, 〜ない; noun / i-adjective く-form / na-adjective + で + こそあれ

senses.label: Only A, never B
senses.meaning: Affirms the first part while strongly denying the opposite. Like “if anything, A; certainly not B”. The second part is usually 「〜ことはない」, 「〜はずがない」 or 「〜ない」.
senses.connection: Action noun / verb masu-stem + こそすれ, 〜はしない／〜ことはない (感謝こそすれ, 増えこそすれ)
examples: I feel nothing but gratitude toward him. I have no resentment at all.
If left alone, this problem will only get worse. It won't solve itself.
The world's population will only keep growing. It's unlikely to suddenly fall.

senses.label: There may be A, but…
senses.meaning: 「〜こそあれ」 often appears in 「程度の差こそあれ」 and 「違いこそあれ」: “there may be differences in…, but (essentially the same)”. Like 「こそすれ」, it can also mean “only A, not B”.
senses.connection: Noun + こそあれ (差こそあれ／違いこそあれ); i-adjective く-form + こそあれ
examples: To varying degrees, everyone has something they're bad at.
They phrase it differently, but the two are making the same argument.
That job was nothing but hard. I never once found it fun.

notes: The second part must be the opposite of the first and be negated; a same-direction clause does not work: ✕「感謝こそすれ、ありがたいと思っている」→ ○「感謝こそすれ、恨むことはない」.
「こそすれ」 attaches to action nouns or the stem (masu-form) of verbs; adjectives take 「こそあれ」: ✕「苦しこそすれ」→ ○「苦しくこそあれ」.
After 「程度の差こそあれ」 comes an affirmative common point (“there are differences of degree, but all…”), not a negation. Do not read it with the 「こそすれ〜ない」 pattern in mind.
The tone is stiff and written. In everyday conversation it sounds affected; in speech say 「感謝することはあっても、恨むことはない」.

daily.title: Reading a news commentary
daily.description: An opinion piece states that a trend will only continue.
daily.example: At this rate, the falling birthrate will only accelerate. It won't stop.

daily.title: Telling a friend how you feel
daily.description: A friend worries you're angry. You sincerely say you're only grateful.
daily.example: A bother? Not at all. I'm only grateful. Why would I be angry?

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Discussing what two different views have in common.
work.example: Though they differ in degree, the two analyses agree.

work.title: Explaining business policy
work.description: Telling employees that conditions will only get tougher.
work.example: Market competition will only intensify from here. It won't ease up.

etymology: Made of the emphatic particle 「こそ」 + the realis forms 「すれ／あれ」 of 「する／ある」. It is a remnant of the classical 「こそ〜realis form」 agreement rule (kakari-musubi). In classical Japanese, 「こそ〜realis form」 followed by a contrast meant “although…”, which led to the “only A, not B” use.

similar.title: 〜こそ
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use the emphatic particle 「こそ」. 「〜こそ」 alone just stresses “precisely…” (「今度こそ」); 「〜こそすれ」 must be followed by a negation of the opposite, meaning “only A, never B”.

similar.title: 〜こそ〜が (concessive)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「こそ〜が」 can be seen as the modern form of the concessive use of 「こそ＋已然形」, meaning “…is true, but…” (「形こそ悪いが味はいい」); 「こそすれ」 puts the weight on negating the opposite of the first part.

formation: 「こそ」 is an emphatic particle, and 「すれ／あれ」 are the realis forms of 「する／ある」. In classical grammar there is a rule of “kakari-musubi”: when 「こそ」 is used in a clause, the predicate takes the realis form; and when 「こそ〜realis form」 continues into the next clause, it makes a concessive “true…, but…”. So 「感謝こそすれ」 = “gratitude there is, to be sure”, followed by “(but) resentment there is not”, which gives “only A, never B”. 「こそ」 singles out A for emphasis, and the second part negates the opposite B, so A and B must run in opposite directions. 「こそあれ」 uses 「ある」, so it attaches to nouns and adjectives and means “… does exist, to be sure”, which gives expressions like 「差こそあれ」 (there is a difference, to be sure).

meaning: Extreme degree: “nothing could be more…, utterly…”. Often expresses the speaker's strong feelings or judgment.
connection: Na-adjective + なこと + この上ない; i-adjective + こと + この上ない

senses.label: Utterly…
senses.meaning: A quality or feeling has reached its peak; nothing could exceed it. Like “extremely…, … in the extreme”. Works for both positive and negative judgments, but negative ones are more common.
senses.connection: Na-adjective + なこと / i-adjective dictionary form + こと + この上ない (危険なこと／失礼なこと／うれしいこと)
examples: Late-night construction is a nuisance in the extreme.
Walking alone at night is extremely dangerous.
Being praised by the teacher I admire made me happier than anything.

senses.label: Direct modification
senses.meaning: Without 「こと」, 「この上ない + noun」 and 「この上なく + adjective」 also mean “supreme, utmost”. Mostly positive, as in 「この上ない喜び」.
senses.connection: この上ない + noun; この上なく + adjective / verb; also 「この上もない」
examples: I feel the utmost joy at winning the championship.
The view from the summit was beautiful beyond compare.

notes: 「この上ない」 means “the very top, nothing beyond”; it is not a negation: 「迷惑なことこの上ない」 means “extremely annoying”. Reading it as “not a nuisance” reverses the meaning.
Na-adjectives need 「な」 before 「こと」: ✕「迷惑ことこの上ない」→ ○「迷惑なことこの上ない」.
Used about another person's words or actions, it is a very harsh negative judgment; saying 「失礼なことこの上ない」 to a boss or client in person is a severe rebuke and very offensive.
「この上は」 and 「この上〜」 mean “in that case” or “on top of this (still more)” (「この上何を望むのか」), which is different from this pattern.

daily.title: Complaining about neighbors
daily.description: Complaining to a friend about noisy neighbors late at night, with exaggeration.
daily.example: A party every night? It's the most annoying thing ever.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's deep sadness.
daily.example: The heart of the boy who had lost his mother was lonely beyond words.

work.title: Award acceptance speech
work.description: Expressing thanks and joy at an awards ceremony.
work.example: It is the greatest honor to receive such an award.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: An editorial criticizes a decision as highly irresponsible.
work.example: Canceling the plan without any explanation is irresponsible in the extreme.

etymology: 「この上」 means “above this”, so 「この上ない」 is literally “there is nothing above this”, i.e. “supreme”. Adding the formal noun 「こと」 in front makes a literary emphasis: “this has reached the limit”.

similar.title: 〜極まる／〜極まりない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “extremely…”. 「極まりない」 attaches directly to the stem of na-adjectives (「失礼極まりない」), is used almost only for negative judgments, and is stronger; 「ことこの上ない」 needs 「なこと」 and works for both positive and negative judgments.

similar.title: 〜の極み
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean reaching the extreme. 「の極み」 attaches to nouns and is used mostly in formal greetings or positive feelings (「光栄の極み」); 「ことこの上ない」 attaches to adjectives and is used more to evaluate things.

similar.title: 〜限りだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「限りだ」 expresses only the speaker's own feeling (「うれしい限りだ」); 「ことこの上ない」 can also objectively evaluate things (「危険なことこの上ない」).

similar.title: 〜の至り
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “extremely…”. 「の至り」 attaches to a few nouns and is mostly a set greeting phrase (「光栄の至り」, 「恐縮の至り」); 「ことこの上ない」 attaches to adjectives and has a wider range.

formation: 「この上」 = 「この」 (this) + 「上」 (above), meaning “above this degree”; 「ない」 denies its existence, so 「この上ない」 means “there is nothing above this”, that is, the highest, the peak. The 「こと」 in front turns the adjective into a noun and forms a subject-predicate relation: “(this) being dangerous / there is nothing beyond it”: 「危険なこと／この上ない」. Because 「こと」 is a noun, na-adjectives connect with 「な」 and i-adjectives modify in the dictionary form. Without 「こと」, 「この上ない」 is itself an adjective and can modify a noun directly (「この上ない喜び」) or modify an adjective as 「この上なく」.

meaning: Missing the chance to do something, so it doesn't get done. Carries a sense of regret.
connection: Verb masu-stem + そびれる (言いそびれる／聞きそびれる／寝そびれる)

senses.label: Missing the chance
senses.meaning: You wanted to (or should have) done it, but the timing or mood wasn't right, so you didn't. Like “didn't get the chance to…, missed the moment to…”. Has a tone of regret.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + そびれる／そびれた／そびれてしまう (言い・聞き・渡し・買い・食べ + そびれる)
examples: I missed my chance to tell her the truth.
I was so busy I missed lunch.
He changed schools before I got the chance to thank him.

senses.label: 寝そびれる
senses.meaning: 「寝そびれる」 is a common combination: you missed the moment to fall asleep and now can't sleep.
senses.connection: 寝 + そびれる
examples: A phone call woke me in the middle of the night, and I couldn't get back to sleep.
I ended up staying up late and missed my chance to sleep.

notes: 「そびれる」 means “meant to do it and should have, but missed the chance”. It is not “could not do” and not “forgot”: ✕「漢字が難しくて読みそびれた」→ ○「漢字が難しくて読めなかった」.
It attaches only to actions the speaker intended to do, not to natural phenomena or involuntary actions: ✕「雨が降りそびれた」.
「寝そびれる」 means “missed the moment to fall asleep, and so cannot sleep”, not “forgot to sleep”.
To thank or inform someone belatedly, 「お礼を言いそびれてしまって、すみません」 is a tactful phrase, softer than saying 「忘れていました」 outright.
It looks like 「そびえる」 (to tower) but is unrelated: 「ビルがそびえる」.

daily.title: Chatting with a friend
daily.description: Talking about something you wanted to ask but never did.
daily.example: I never got the chance to ask for his contact info.

daily.title: Missing out on a purchase
daily.description: The item you wanted is sold out.
daily.example: I missed out on the limited-edition cake. What a shame.

daily.title: Explaining a late night to family
daily.description: Very sleepy in the morning, explaining why to your family.
daily.example: I couldn't fall asleep last night, so I'm terribly sleepy this morning.

work.title: Apologizing to a colleague
work.description: Admitting you didn't get to hand over some documents.
work.example: Sorry, I didn't get a chance to give you the documents at the meeting.

work.title: Follow-up questions
work.description: Emailing after a meeting to ask what you didn't get to ask.
work.example: I'd like to confirm a point I didn't get to ask about in the meeting earlier.

etymology: The origin of 「そびれる」 is unclear. In modern Japanese it is only used as an auxiliary verb after the masu-stem, meaning “to miss the chance and fail to do”. It is usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜損なう・〜損ねる・〜損じる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜損ねる」 too can mean “missed the chance and did not manage” (「見損ねる」). But 「損なう」 can also mean “did it wrongly, ruined it” (「書き損じる」), whereas 「そびれる」 only means not having done it because the moment was missed, and is more colloquial.

similar.title: 〜ずじまい
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean not having managed to do it. 「〜ずじまい」 stresses the outcome “in the end, never…” (「会えずじまい」); 「〜そびれる」 stresses that the cause was “missing the timing”, and a chance may still come later.

formation: The structure is verb stem (masu-form) + 「そびれる」, a compound verb: the first part is the action one wanted to do, and the second part 「そびれる」 adds the sense “missed the timing and did not manage”. The etymology of 「そびれる」 itself is unclear and in modern Japanese it is used only as an auxiliary element, so it is usually written in kana. Since it means “being out of step with the right moment”, it presupposes that the person originally intended to do the action, which is why it carries a tone of regret and attaches only to volitional actions. 「寝そびれる」 follows the same logic: you missed the moment when you wanted to sleep, and as a result you cannot sleep.

meaning: Things aren't ideal, but compared with something worse, this one point is still good. Has a self-consoling tone.
connection: Plain form + だけましだ (na-adjective: 〜なだけましだ; noun: 〜であるだけましだ)

senses.label: At least…
senses.meaning: The overall situation is bad, but you find one “still OK” point to comfort yourself or others. Like “at least…, it's a good thing that…”. Often said with 「まだ」: 「〜だけまだましだ」.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form + だけ（まだ）ましだ; often follows 「〜が／〜けど」
examples: The pay is low, but at least I have a job.
I have a high fever, but at least I still have an appetite.
My wallet was stolen, but let's just be glad my passport is safe.

senses.label: Better than…
senses.meaning: Compared with a worse case, you admit that this is “not great, but at least better”. Often used with 「〜よりは」 or 「〜でも」.
senses.connection: 〜よりは + verb plain form + だけましだ; 〜だけでもましだ
examples: Doing even a little is better than doing nothing.
Even if the reply is late, it's something that it comes at all.

notes: 「まし」 only means “a bit better than something worse”; it is not praise. Telling someone about their work or gift 「〜だけましだ」 amounts to “it is poor, but passable” and is hurtful and rude.
Saying 「〜だけましじゃない」 directly to someone who has suffered a misfortune sounds as though you take their pain lightly; to elders or clients, use 「〜だけでも不幸中の幸いでした」.
After a noun you cannot attach 「だけ」 directly: ✕「軽傷だけましだ」 (it would mean “only the minor injury part”) → ○「軽傷で済んだだけましだ」.
Do not confuse it with 「〜ほうがましだ」: 「ほうがましだ」 chooses between two bad options (「行くくらいなら死んだほうがましだ」), whereas 「だけましだ」 finds one thing to be thankful for within a bad situation that has already occurred.

daily.title: Bad weather on a trip
daily.description: It rains on a trip, and friends console each other.
daily.example: It's raining, but at least it's not a typhoon.

daily.title: Disappointing test score
daily.description: A bad score, but not a fail. Consoling yourself.
daily.example: My score was bad, but at least I didn't fail, I guess.

work.title: Project delay
work.description: The project is delayed but not canceled. Colleagues console each other.
work.example: The deadline was pushed back, but at least the contract wasn't terminated.

work.title: Disaster news report
work.description: A report mentions the one fortunate point in a disaster.
work.example: Damage to buildings was severe, but at least there were no deaths.

etymology: 「まし」 is written 「増し」 and originally meant “increase, more”. It came to mean “(of two) better, passable”. 「だけ」 means “just this point”, so together: “on this point alone, it's still better”.

similar.title: 〜ほうがましだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「まし」 (relatively better). 「ほうがましだ」 compares two options that are both bad, meaning “rather than…, better to…”; 「だけましだ」 finds one thing to be thankful for in a bad present situation and makes no choice.

similar.title: 〜からいいようなものの
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are “it's a good thing that…”. 「からいいようなものの」 adds a reproach or warning after the relief (“luckily nothing happened, but you were too careless”); 「だけましだ」 is self-consolation and stops there, without reproach.

similar.title: 〜ならまだしも
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are relative judgments of “still acceptable”. 「ならまだしも」 means “if it were A it would be fine, but (the actual) B is not”, putting the weight on criticizing B; 「だけましだ」 means “things are bad, but this one point is still good”, putting the weight on consolation.

formation: 「だけ」 limits the range, meaning “on this point alone”; 「まし」 was originally written 「増し」, with the original sense “increase, a cut above”, extended to “a little better (when two things are compared)”. Combined, it means “on this point alone, a little better (than a worse case)”. 「だけ」 limits the range to one point, implying everything else is bad, and 「まし」 is “better” in a comparative sense, not absolutely “good”. So the whole sentence naturally carries a turn of “overall it is bad, but…” and a tone of self-consolation, and often goes with 「〜が」 or 「〜けど」.

meaning: “Has never once…”. Often used to criticize or complain that someone or something is always this way.
connection: Verb ta-form + ためしがない

senses.label: Never once
senses.meaning: This has never happened in the past. Stresses “not even once” with dissatisfaction or resignation. Mostly used to criticize others, but also for self-mockery.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ためしがない／ためしはない／ためしがありません
examples: He has never once shown up on time.
My sister starts diets, but she's never once stuck with one.
I've bought lottery tickets many times, but I've never won.

notes: It carries strong dissatisfaction, so used about others it is criticism: saying 「部長が時間通りに来たためしがない」 in front of your boss is very rude. To state a plain fact, use 「〜たことがない」.
It attaches only to the ta-form of verbs: ✕「行くためしがない」→ ○「行ったためしがない」.
This 「ためし」 means “precedent”, different from the “trying” in 「試しに使ってみる」 (try using it). Do not read it as “have not tried”.
Used about your own good record it sounds boastful (「私は試験に落ちたためしがない」) and comes across as arrogant where modesty is expected; to say it neutrally, use 「一度も〜たことがない」.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: Complaining to a friend that your husband never keeps his word.
daily.example: My husband says he'll help, but he's never actually helped once.

daily.title: Self-mockery
daily.description: Talking about your own short-lived enthusiasm.
daily.example: Even when I start a diary, I've never kept it up for a week.

work.title: Complaining about a supplier
work.description: Colleagues complain that a supplier always delivers late.
work.example: That supplier has never once met a deadline.

work.title: Criticizing failed forecasts
work.description: A commentator criticizes a type of forecast that is always wrong.
work.example: Optimistic forecasts of this kind have never once been right.

etymology: 「ためし」 is written 「例し」 and means “precedent, example”. It shares its root with the verb 「ためす（試す）」 and originally meant “an example to rely on”. 「〜たためしがない」 literally means “there is no precedent of…”, hence “has never…”.

similar.title: 〜たことがある
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: its negative 「〜たことがない」 also means “have never…”, but it merely states experience objectively; 「〜たためしがない」 stresses “not once, always so” and carries dissatisfaction or criticism.

similar.title: 〜として〜ない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「一度として〜ない」 is also a strong, total negation meaning “not even once”, neutral in tone and written; 「〜たためしがない」 is more colloquial and carries the speaker's complaint about the other person's consistent behavior.

formation: 「ためし」 is a noun meaning “precedent, instance”, generally thought to share its origin with the verb 「試す」. 「verb ta-form + ためし」 = “a precedent of having… in the past”, and with 「がない」 it becomes “there is not even one precedent of having…”. Using “precedent” rather than “experience” (「こと」) puts the focus on “many times in the past, without a single exception”, so it is stronger than 「〜たことがない」 and naturally brings out the dissatisfaction that “this person / this thing is always like that”. And because it speaks of past precedent, only the ta-form can precede it.

meaning: Explains the reason or premise behind an action: “it's because of… that (I/they did it).”
connection: Verb te-form + のことだ (〜を思ってのことだ／〜があってのことだ)

senses.label: Out of concern for…
senses.meaning: Explains that an action that seems unusual actually comes from a certain thought or motive. Like “it's because… / it's out of concern for…”. Often used to defend or explain someone's behavior.
senses.connection: 「AのはBてのことだ」: 思って／考えて／心配して／期待して + のことだ
examples: When I say harsh things, it's because I'm thinking of your future.
He quit his job after careful thought.
My mother keeps calling probably because she's worried about me.

senses.label: Based on…
senses.meaning: Explains that something happened under a certain cause or condition. Like “it's because of…, it's in response to…”. Common in news and explanatory texts.
senses.connection: 〜を受けて／〜があって／〜を踏まえて + のことだ (のことで)
examples: This price increase is reportedly in response to soaring raw material costs.
The manager must have had some reason for postponing the meeting.

notes: The first part is a motive that was thought through, or an objective background; it is not used for accidental slips or a plain cause: ✕「遅れたのは寝坊してのことです」→ ○「遅れたのは寝坊したからです」.
「あなたのためを思ってのことだ」 is fine to a junior, but to a superior it sounds like a favor you are doing them and comes across as condescending; to a superior, explain your intention with 「〜と思いまして」.
In 「旅行でのことだ」 or 「彼についてのことです」, the 「の」 follows a particle and means “the matter at the time of…” or “the matter concerning…”; that is not this pattern.

daily.title: Defending someone's parents
daily.description: A child complains about strict parents, and someone takes the parents' side.
daily.example: Your parents are strict because they're thinking of what's best for you.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: The news explains someone's decision.
daily.example: The athlete's retirement reportedly came in light of his worsening injury.

work.title: Explaining a decision to a subordinate
work.description: A boss explains the intention behind a personnel change.
work.example: This transfer is because we hope you'll make use of your experience.

work.title: Public announcement
work.description: A company explains a price change in a notice.
work.example: This price revision reflects the rise in logistics costs.

etymology: Made of verb te-form + the particle 「の」 + the formal noun 「こと」 + 「だ」. 「〜ての + noun」 means “(noun) based on…”, so 「〜てのこと」 is “a matter based on…”, used to explain the starting point of an action.

similar.title: 〜のは〜からだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both state an action and then give the reason. 「〜からだ」 just explains the cause in general; 「〜てのことだ」 stresses the thought or premise behind the action and often carries a tone of defending or sympathizing with the person.

similar.title: 〜あっての
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜があってのことだ」 is itself a common phrase. 「あっての」 attaches to nouns and stresses an indispensable premise, “B exists only because of A” (「客あっての商売」); 「〜てのことだ」 attaches to various verb te-forms and explains the starting point of an action.

similar.title: 〜からこそ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both highlight the cause. 「からこそ」 stresses “precisely because…” and puts the cause first; 「〜てのことだ」 comes at the end of the sentence and adds the motive for an action already mentioned.

formation: It is formed from verb te-form + 「の」 + 「こと」 + 「だ」. The te-form here means “on the premise of…, in the state of…”, and 「〜ての＋noun」 means “a (noun) based on…”, as in 「熟慮しての決断」 (a decision made after careful thought). Replace the noun with the formal noun 「こと」 and 「〜てのことだ」 means “that is a matter based on…”. So it always comes at the end of the sentence and looks back to explain an action already mentioned: “(he did that) out of…”. Because it focuses on “the starting point behind the action”, it is often used to explain that someone's seemingly odd behavior actually had a purpose.

meaning: A literary form of 「〜ではないだろうか」. Gently expresses a guess or opinion: “isn't it perhaps…?”
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + ではなかろうか; verb / i-adjective plain form + のではなかろうか

senses.label: Tentative guess
senses.meaning: Expresses a guess as a question: “might it not be…?, perhaps…”. It avoids a direct statement and sounds careful and soft. Common in papers, commentaries and speeches.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + ではなかろうか
examples: Might the cause simply be an operating error?
Isn't now precisely the time to rethink how we work?

senses.label: Tentative claim
senses.meaning: After verbs and adjectives, add 「の」: 「〜のではなかろうか」. Used to put forward your view gently, though the speaker is actually fairly sure.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + のではなかろうか
examples: Isn't this plan a bit unrealistic?
Perhaps there's some truth in what he says.
Young people's drift away from reading may well continue to grow.

notes: The form is a negative question, but the meaning is an affirmative claim: 「原因はミスではなかろうか」 means “I think the cause is a mistake”, not “the cause isn't a mistake, is it?”. Reading it as negative reverses the meaning.
Verbs and i-adjectives need 「の」: ✕「無理があるではなかろうか」→ ○「無理があるのではなかろうか」.
It is very literary and old-fashioned; in everyday talk or spoken to a superior it sounds stiff and affected. In speech use 「〜のではないでしょうか」.
Without 「か」, 「〜なかろう」 is just a negative conjecture: 「雨は降らなかろう」 means “it probably won't rain” and carries no softened-assertion sense.

daily.title: Reading an opinion piece
daily.description: A newspaper columnist gently puts forward a view.
daily.example: What children need is perhaps free time rather than cram school.

daily.title: Reading a book
daily.description: An essayist reflects on life.
daily.example: Happiness may be closer at hand than we think.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper proposes a hypothesis.
work.example: This result may be due to differences in survey methods.

work.title: Raising an objection in a meeting
work.description: Politely expressing a different view in a formal meeting.
work.example: I believe this point may need to be reconsidered.

etymology: 「なかろう」 comes from 「なから」, an old irrealis form of the adjective 「ない」, + the volitional/conjectural auxiliary 「う」. It equals 「ないだろう」. Adding the question particle 「か」 gives the soft guess “isn't it…?”.

similar.title: 〜のではないだろうか
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning: 「なかろう」 is the archaic form of 「ないだろう」. 「ではないだろうか」 is common in modern writing and speech; 「ではなかろうか」 is stiffer and appears mostly in papers and commentary.

similar.title: 〜ではあるまいか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are written, softened conjectures. 「ではあるまいか」 uses the negative conjectural 「まい」, which is more refined and classical, and appears mostly in literature.

similar.title: 〜のではないか・〜んじゃない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express a conjecture or opinion softly in the form of a rhetorical question. 「〜のではないか」 can be used in speech (「〜んじゃない？」); 「〜ではなかろうか」 is used only in writing.

formation: It is 「では」 + 「なかろう」 + 「か」. 「なかろう」 is the classical stem 「なから」 of 「ない」 plus the conjectural 「う」, equivalent to 「ないだろう」; the whole thing is “it isn't…, is it? + the question 「か」”. By throwing a negative question, “isn't it…?”, to the other person for confirmation, it in effect says “I think it is…”, while sounding modest and careful; that is where its “softened assertion” comes from. Since the archaic 「なかろう」 is kept, it is more literary than 「ではないだろうか」 and has the tone of a paper.

meaning: Lists two judgments or feelings: “should I call it A, or B…?” Hard to sum up in one word.
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem / plain form + というか + noun / na-adjective stem / plain form + というか

senses.label: Is it A, or B…?
senses.meaning: When describing someone or something, two words come to mind, but neither fits perfectly, so you give both. Like “I don't know if it's A or B”. Expresses the speaker's impression, often with surprise or exasperation.
senses.connection: AというかBというか、〜 (A and B are usually evaluative nouns, na-adjectives or adjectives)
examples: Bold or reckless, I can't say, but his actions always surprise me.
Is she honest, or just naive? She believes whatever people tell her.
Going abroad alone? I don't know if that's brave or just reckless.

senses.label: Hard to put into words
senses.meaning: Used for complex, mixed feelings: give two feelings side by side, or say 「〜というか何というか」, meaning “I don't know how to describe it.”
senses.connection: Emotion adjective + というか + emotion adjective + というか; 〜というか何というか
examples: Happy, embarrassed… it's a complicated feeling.
Surprised, or whatever you call it, I was speechless.

notes: A and B are two ways of describing the same thing; the pattern cannot list different things: ✕「彼は英語というか数学というか、何でも得意だ」→ ○「彼は英語といい数学といい、何でも得意だ」.
It often carries a negative or mixed judgment of the person (「図々しいというか無神経というか」), so used about a boss's or client's behavior it is rude.

A lone 「というか／っていうか」 means “or rather” or “come to think of it”, and in speech it is often used to change the subject. Starting sentences with 「っていうか」 over and over in formal settings sounds childish and impolite.

daily.title: Describing a friend
daily.description: Talking with a friend about an acquaintance with a unique personality.
daily.example: Tanaka is so… laid-back? Free-spirited? Anyway, he's an interesting guy.

daily.title: Talking about a movie
daily.description: After seeing a movie, telling a friend about feelings that are hard to describe.
daily.example: That movie was scary, or sad, or something. It was a strange film.

work.title: Evaluating a proposal
work.description: Colleagues privately discuss a bold proposal.
work.example: This proposal is innovative, or maybe just eccentric. Opinions will probably be split.

work.title: Talking in an interview
work.description: An athlete describes their feelings after winning.
work.example: I'm relieved, or I can't believe it… It hasn't really sunk in yet.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + 「いう」 (say) + the question particle 「か」. Literally “should I say…?”. Repeated twice, it shows hesitation: neither A nor B is quite right.

similar.title: 〜というか (standalone)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「と＋いう＋か」. A lone 「というか」 is used to correct or revise one's wording (「疲れたというか、もう限界だ」), settling finally on the latter wording; 「〜というか〜というか」 lines up two wordings without choosing.

similar.title: 〜というより
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are used to weigh one's wording. 「AというよりB」 clearly means “rather than A, B”, settling on B; 「〜というか〜というか」 hesitates between two wordings, neither of which is quite right.

similar.title: 〜といい〜といい
similar.explanation: Often compared. 「AといいBといい」 lists two different aspects, and the second part is a single overall evaluation (「味といい値段といい申し分ない」); 「〜というか〜というか」 gives two evaluations of the same thing, showing it is hard to sum up.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can line up feelings. 「〜やら〜やら」 means “both… and…”, several states existing at once (「うれしいやら恥ずかしいやら」); 「〜というか〜というか」 stresses “not knowing which word describes it”.

formation: It is 「と」 (quotation) + 「いう」 (say) + 「か」 (question), literally “should one say…?”. The speaker gives wording A and marks it uncertain with 「か」; then gives wording B and puts the same question mark on it. Lining up two questioned wordings expresses hesitation: “saying A is not right, and saying B is not entirely right either”, conveying the feeling that it is hard to sum up in a word. Since the core is “how to put it”, A and B must be different wordings for the same thing, not a list of different things; the sentence often trails off afterward precisely because it is “hard to put into words”.

meaning: “It's no exaggeration to say…”. Stresses that a judgment is fully justified.
connection: Noun / plain form + と言っても過言ではない

senses.label: No exaggeration to say…
senses.meaning: The speaker gives a very strong judgment and stresses that it isn't an exaggeration. Like “it's no exaggeration to say…”. Formal; common in speeches, news and commentary.
senses.connection: Noun (だ) / plain form + と言っても過言ではない／過言ではありません／過言ではないだろう
examples: It's no exaggeration to say this discovery changed the history of medicine.
It's no exaggeration to call him the leading figure in this industry.
It's probably no exaggeration to say sleep determines your health.

senses.label: 言い過ぎではない
senses.meaning: The same idea can be said as 「〜と言っても言い過ぎではない」, which is slightly more conversational.
senses.connection: Plain form + と言っても言い過ぎではない
examples: It's no overstatement to say this shop's ramen is the best in Japan.

notes: 「過言ではない」 means “is not an exaggeration”, so the whole sentence is a strong affirmation, not a negation. Reading it as “it is wrong to say so” reverses the meaning.
The first part must be a very high evaluation; attached to a plain fact it sounds odd: ✕「彼は会社員だと言っても過言ではない」.
In interviews, self-introductions and other settings that call for modesty, using it about yourself or your own company sounds boastful and arrogant: ✕「私はこの分野の第一人者と言っても過言ではありません」.
「過言」 is read 「かごん」, not 「かげん」.

daily.title: Recommending something to a friend
daily.description: Enthusiastically recommending a book to a friend.
daily.example: It's no exaggeration to say this novel changed my life.

daily.title: Reading sports news
daily.description: The news praises an athlete's great achievements.
daily.example: It's no exaggeration to say he is the history of Japanese soccer itself.

work.title: Company speech
work.description: The president stresses the importance of employees in a speech.
work.example: It is no exaggeration to say our company's growth is thanks to the efforts of every single employee.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper stresses the key role of a technology.
work.example: It is no exaggeration to say this technology is the foundation of modern society.

etymology: 「過言」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “words that go too far, exaggeration”. Literally the phrase means “even if you say this, it is not an exaggeration”, which adds weight to the judgment.

similar.title: 〜と言ってもいい
similar.explanation: Same origin: both have the structure 「と言っても」 + evaluation. 「と言ってもいい」 means “you can say…”, is milder and is common in speech; 「と言っても過言ではない」 stresses “not an exaggeration at all”, a stronger and more formal evaluation.

similar.title: 〜と言える
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are used to make an evaluation. 「と言える」 is a fairly objective, calm conclusion (“it can be said that…”); 「と言っても過言ではない」 carries the speaker's strong subjective emphasis.

formation: Taken apart, it is 「と言っても」 + 「過言」 + 「ではない」. 「と言っても」 is the quotation 「と」 + the te-form of 「言う」 + the concessive 「も」, meaning “even if one says so”; 「過言」 is “words that go too far”; and 「ではない」 negates it. Together: “even if one says…, it is not going too far”. It first presupposes that “some might find this an exaggeration” and then denies that exaggeration, thereby stressing that the evaluation is just right. Precisely because the structure presupposes “might be taken as an exaggeration”, the first part must be a very high evaluation.

meaning: A classical auxiliary expressing duty or command (should, must), and also naturalness or possibility. Today mostly used in slogans, rules or humorous exclamations.
connection: Verb dictionary form + べし (する → すべし／するべし)

senses.label: Should / must
senses.meaning: Expresses duty or a command, like 「〜なければならない」 or 「〜せよ」. Firm and concise. Common in rules, slogans, admonitions and notices.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べし; 「する」 usually becomes 「すべし」
examples: Always be on time for appointments.
Hard hats must be worn during work.
Students shall devote themselves to their studies.

senses.label: Easy to imagine
senses.meaning: Expresses naturalness or possibility: “can…, should naturally…”. Today it mainly appears in the idiom 「推して知るべし」 (“you can imagine”).
senses.connection: 推して知る + べし
examples: You can imagine how hard it was for him.
With preparations in this state, you can guess the result.

senses.label: Scary good
senses.meaning: 「Noun + 恐るべし」 is an exclamation: “… is formidable, not to be underestimated”. A humorous expression common in modern speech and online.
senses.connection: Noun (、) + 恐るべし
examples: Kids these days are something else.
The power of the internet to spread things is scary.

notes: 「べし」 sounds like a command and is used only in rules, slogans or self-encouragement; saying 「〜すべし」 to a boss or client is extremely arrogant and rude.
Before a noun it becomes 「べき」: ✕「守るべし約束」→ ○「守るべき約束」.
The negative is not 「べしない」 but 「べからず」 (“must not”): ✕「入るべしない」→ ○「入るべからず」.
「〜恐るべし」 is a humorous exclamation with a teasing tone, so avoid it in formal settings or with elders.

daily.title: An exclamation online
daily.description: Marveling on social media at how powerful something is.
daily.example: This restaurant's large portion is terrifying.

daily.title: Reading manga
daily.description: A master in a manga lectures in an old-fashioned tone.

etymology: 「べし」 was one of the most common auxiliaries in classical Japanese, expressing conjecture, will, naturalness, duty, command, possibility and more. It is generally thought to come from the adverb 「うべ（宜）」, “naturally, rightly”. Modern 「べきだ」, 「べからず」 and 「べく」 are all forms of it.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「べき」 is the attributive form of 「べし」. 「べきだ」 is modern Japanese and expresses general advice or assertion (「もっと勉強すべきだ」); 「べし」 is the classical terminal form, firmer and more archaic, and appears mostly in slogans and rules.

similar.title: 〜べからず／〜べからざる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「べからず」 is the negative of 「べし」 and expresses prohibition, “must not…” (「芝生に入るべからず」); 「べし」 means “must…”.

similar.title: 〜べく
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「べく」 is the continuative form of 「べし」 and expresses purpose, “in order to…” (「合格すべく努力する」); 「べし」 at the end of a sentence expresses obligation or command.

similar.title: 〜ねばならない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are written expressions of obligation. 「ねばならない」 states “must…”; 「べし」 is shorter and has the tone of a command or admonition.

formation: 「べし」 is a classical auxiliary that attaches to the terminal form of verbs (in modern terms, the dictionary form). Its original sense is “natural, as it should be”, thought to be related to 「うべ（宜）」, which means “indeed so”. When “natural” develops in the direction of the speaker's will, it becomes “must, ought” (obligation, command); in the direction of judgment, it becomes “may, reasonably” (naturalness, possibility), so 「推して知るべし」 = “if you infer it, you should understand”. It conjugates like an adjective, with attributive 「べき」, continuative 「べく」 and negative 「べからず」; the modern 「べきだ」, 「べく」 and 「べからず」 all come from it.

meaning: “Without regard for…”: acting without considering danger, consequences or other people.
connection: Noun + を顧みず／も顧みず

senses.label: Regardless of danger
senses.meaning: Acting bravely without regard for one's own safety. Often used to praise someone's courage. Common with 「危険」, 「身の危険」, 「自分の命」.
senses.connection: 危険／身の危険／命 + を顧みず・も顧みず
examples: Without regard for the danger, the firefighter rushed into the burning house.
With no thought for his own safety, he saved a child who had fallen into the river.

senses.label: Ignoring others / consequences
senses.meaning: Ignoring one's family, the people around, or possible consequences. When critical, it means “thinking only of oneself, reckless”.
senses.connection: 家庭／周囲の迷惑／健康／結果 + を顧みず・も顧みず
examples: My father neglected his family and did nothing but work.
Some people talk loudly on the train without any regard for those around them.
He kept working with no regard for his health, and eventually collapsed.

notes: Whether it praises or blames depends on the object: 「危険を顧みず」 praises selfless courage, while 「家庭を顧みず」 criticizes irresponsibility. Change the object and the evaluation reverses.
It is a homophone of 「省みる」 (to reflect on oneself) with a different meaning: to say “without reflecting on oneself”, write 「自らを省みず」; written as 「顧みず」 it becomes “disregarding oneself”.
The first part should be something weighty that one ought to consider (danger, health, family, other people); with trivial things it sounds exaggerated: ✕「値段を顧みず買った」→ ○「値段も気にせず買った」.
It is written language; in speech people usually say 「〜も気にしないで」 or 「〜もかまわずに」.

etymology: 「顧みる」 is made of 「かえり（返り）」 + 「みる（見る）」, originally “to look back”, extended to “to care about”. 「ず」 is the classical negative auxiliary, so 「顧みず」 is “without looking back”, i.e. “without regard for”.

similar.title: 〜もかまわず
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “without regard to…”. 「もかまわず」 mostly means not minding others' eyes or the surroundings (「人目もかまわず泣く」) and is more colloquial; 「を顧みず」 is used for weighty matters such as danger, family or health, and is more written.

similar.title: 〜をものともせず
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「をものともせず」 means not treating difficulties as a big deal and bravely overcoming them, and is used only to praise; 「を顧みず」 means not taking into account, and can praise or blame.

similar.title: 〜をよそに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「をよそに」 means ignoring the surrounding people's worry, opposition and so on (「親の心配をよそに」), and is mostly critical; 「を顧みず」 focuses on disregarding one's own danger or the responsibility one should bear.

similar.title: 〜を押して
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean acting in spite of unfavorable conditions. 「を押して」 often follows illness, opposition and the like, meaning “pushing on, braving it” (「病を押して出席する」); 「を顧みず」 stresses “not considering” the consequences.

formation: 「顧みる」 is built from 「かえり（返り）」 + 「みる（見る）」, originally “to look back”, extended to “to take into account, to care about”. 「ず」 is the classical negative auxiliary, so 「顧みず」 means “without looking back (but charging ahead)”, that is, “disregarding”. With 「を」 the object is “not taking… into account”; replacing it with 「も」 gives “not even… taken into account”, a stronger tone. Because what one “looks back at” is usually something one should be concerned about (danger, one's body, one's family), the pattern can describe both selfless courage and reckless disregard.

meaning: Doing something that deserves proper attention only half-heartedly, then rushing on to the next thing.

senses.label: Hurriedly…, then
senses.meaning: The first action (a greeting, a meal, preparations) should be done properly, but because of haste it's done only roughly before jumping to the next. Like “barely…before…, cutting… short to…”. Has a hurried, impatient feel.
senses.connection: 挨拶／食事／朝ご飯／準備 + もそこそこに + action
examples: He cut the greetings short and got straight to the point.
The children hardly ate before running outside to play.
I gulped down breakfast and dashed out of the house.

notes: It differs from 「そこそこ」 used alone (“decent, passable”): 「そこそこおいしい」 is praise, but 「食事もそこそこに」 means not eating properly. Mixing them up changes the meaning completely.
It attaches only to nouns: ✕「食べるもそこそこに」→ ○「食事もそこそこに」.
In Japan, skipping greetings and getting straight to business is easily seen as impatient or rude; in business settings people soften it first with 「ご挨拶もそこそこに恐縮ですが、…」.

etymology: 「そこそこ」 was originally an adverb meaning “hastily, roughly”. It is thought to be a doubling of the demonstrative 「そこ」, meaning “up to there is enough”. 「Noun + もそこそこに」 means “even… is done only roughly”.

similar.title: 〜や否や／〜や
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both describe hurried, immediately successive actions. 「や否や」 stresses that two things happen almost at the same time (「ベルが鳴るや否や飛び出した」); 「もそこそこに」 stresses that the first part was not done properly because of hurrying to the second.

similar.title: 〜が早いか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「が早いか」 attaches to the dictionary form of verbs and means the second event follows the instant the action occurs; 「もそこそこに」 attaches to nouns and the point is that the first part was done perfunctorily.

similar.title: 〜なり (as soon as)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「なり」 attaches to verbs and means “as soon as…”, with the second part often an unexpected action (「顔を見るなり泣き出した」); 「もそこそこに」 focuses on the first part being done sloppily and in a hurry.

formation: 「も」 is “even…”, 「そこそこ」 is an adverb meaning “perfunctorily, doing it only to that extent and leaving it”, and 「に」 makes it modify the action that follows. Together: “even (what should have been done properly)… was only done perfunctorily, and then…”. 「も」 implies that the first part should have been done seriously, and 「そこそこ」 means it was done only to the “good enough” point before stopping, which naturally leads to a second part of “hurrying on to the next thing”, bringing out a sense of haste and impatience.
